items.stem: Which term describes the growing proportion of women in paid work, especially in global manufacturing and services?
items.answer: Feminisation of employment
items.markingKey: Feminisation of employment: the growing proportion of women in paid work, especially in global manufacturing and services. [1]

items.stem: What is meant by the term “feminisation of employment”? Give one example.
items.answer: The growing proportion of women in paid work, especially in global manufacturing and services. Example: young women making up most workers in export factories.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition (the growing proportion of women in paid work, especially in global manufacturing and services); 1 mark for a relevant example such as young women making up most workers in export factories. [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between “informal sector” and “global care chain”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Informal sector: work that is unregulated, unprotected and often unrecorded (e.g. street vending and home-based piecework). Global care chain: a series of links between people across the world based on paid or unpaid care work (e.g. a migrant nanny caring for children abroad while her own children are cared for by relatives).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: Zara, aged 19, moved from her village to work in a garment factory near Lima; she works 60 hours a week, sends money home and now helps decide how her family spends it. Suggest how a neoliberal sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Neoliberalism: factory jobs created by free trade give women opportunities and income that would not otherwise exist.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: A factory supplying a global fashion brand near Doha employs 3,000 women on machines, while all its supervisors and managers are men. Explain how a liberal feminist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Liberal feminism: paid work gives women income, independence and bargaining power; improved rights and education can reduce inequality (Kabeer).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Assess how useful longitudinal studies (following the same sample over time) are for studying the changing share of women in global employment.
items.answer: Strengths: they are ideal for tracking change in the same individuals or families over many years; they can combine quantitative and qualitative data. Limitations: sample attrition (people dropping out) can make the sample unrepresentative over time; they are very expensive and results take many years to appear. Theory: longitudinal studies (following the same sample over time) are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce mainly quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the changing share of women in global employment but best combined with another method such as case studies (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Which term describes the growing proportion of women in paid work, especially in global manufacturing and services?
items.answer: Feminisation of employment
items.markingKey: Feminisation of employment: the growing proportion of women in paid work, especially in global manufacturing and services. [1]

items.stem: Explain what sociologists mean by “double burden”.
items.answer: The combination of paid work and unpaid domestic labour carried out by many women.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition: the combination of paid work and unpaid domestic labour carried out by many women. [1]

items.stem: Distinguish between “export processing zone (EPZ)” and “feminisation of employment”.
items.answer: Export processing zone (EPZ): an area where TNCs set up factories for export with tax breaks and weak regulation. Feminisation of employment: the growing proportion of women in paid work, especially in global manufacturing and services.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for each accurate definition, showing the contrast. [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between “double burden” and “informal sector”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Double burden: the combination of paid work and unpaid domestic labour carried out by many women (e.g. a factory worker who also does all the housework). Informal sector: work that is unregulated, unprotected and often unrecorded (e.g. street vending and home-based piecework).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: Tomás is planning a study of the experiences of women working in export factories. Explain one limitation of using field experiments for this research.
items.answer: Deceiving people about sensitive matters may cause harm or distress.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying a relevant limitation; 1 mark for explaining it in the context of the experiences of women working in export factories. [2]

items.stem: Nadia, aged 19, moved from her village to work in a garment factory near Manila; she works 60 hours a week, sends money home and now helps decide how her family spends it. Explain how liberal feminist and radical feminist sociologists might differ in the way they interpret this situation.
items.answer: Liberal feminism: paid work gives women income, independence and bargaining power; improved rights and education can reduce inequality (Kabeer). Radical feminism: patriarchy continues in the factory: men control women as supervisors, and women still carry the double burden at home.
items.markingKey: Up to 3 marks for each perspective: 1 mark for its key idea, 1 mark for applying it to the situation, 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. 1 further mark for a clear point of contrast is included within the 6. [6]

items.stem: The table shows official employment data from a country near Mumbai with large export factories. Table: percentage of workers who are women | 1995 | 2020. Garment manufacturing | 67% | 75%. Electronics assembly | 51% | 64%. Factory supervisors and managers | 14% | 17%. (a) Calculate the change, in percentage points, for Electronics assembly between 1995 and 2020. (b) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that globalisation has improved women’s position in the labour market.
items.answer: (a) 64 − 51 = +13 percentage points. (b) Evidence from the data: The figure rose for Garment manufacturing, Electronics assembly, Factory supervisors and managers; Garment manufacturing had the highest figure for 2020. Export industries have grown. Qualifications: More jobs do not mean better pay or conditions; women remain under-represented in management; informal work is not recorded. The data also come from official statistics of 3 workers in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for using 51 and 64; 1 mark for +13 percentage points (sign or “rise/fall” needed). [2] (b) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or own knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses the data and own knowledge to argue for and against, with a judgement. [4]

items.stem: Which term describes the process by which people gain power and control over their own lives and choices?
items.answer: Empowerment
items.markingKey: Empowerment: the process by which people gain power and control over their own lives and choices. [1]

items.stem: What is meant by the term “empowerment”? Give one example.
items.answer: The process by which people gain power and control over their own lives and choices. Example: women gaining the right to own land.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition (the process by which people gain power and control over their own lives and choices); 1 mark for a relevant example such as women gaining the right to own land. [2]

items.stem: Distinguish between “Gender and Development (GAD)” and “maternal mortality”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Gender and Development (GAD): an approach focusing on changing unequal gender relations rather than just including women (e.g. projects challenging men’s control of household income). Maternal mortality: deaths of women from causes related to pregnancy and childbirth (e.g. deaths per 100,000 live births).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: A government near Jakarta introduces free secondary schooling for girls; ten years later, the average age of marriage has risen and family size has fallen. Suggest how a radical feminist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Radical feminism: development projects do not challenge patriarchy; men often control women’s loans and income, so real empowerment requires changing gender relations.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: A government near Nairobi introduces free secondary schooling for girls; ten years later, the average age of marriage has risen and family size has fallen. Explain how a neoliberal sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Neoliberalism: microfinance and markets allow women to become entrepreneurs, reducing poverty through self-help (Yunus).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using field experiments to research the effects of microfinance on women’s lives.
items.answer: Strengths: participants usually do not know they are part of an experiment, so they act naturally; one variable can be altered (for example the name on a job application) to test its effect. Limitations: participants have not given informed consent, which raises ethical issues; the researcher has much less control over variables than in a laboratory. Theory: field experiments are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the effects of microfinance on women’s lives but best combined with another method such as personal documents (diaries, letters, blogs and social media posts) (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: What is meant by the term “Gender Inequality Index (GII)”?
items.answer: A UN measure of gender inequality in health, empowerment and the labour market.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition: a UN measure of gender inequality in health, empowerment and the labour market. [1]

items.stem: Distinguish between “Gender and Development (GAD)” and “Women in Development (WID)”.
items.answer: Gender and Development (GAD): an approach focusing on changing unequal gender relations rather than just including women. Women in Development (WID): an approach that aimed to include women in existing development projects.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for each accurate definition, showing the contrast. [2]

items.stem: Explain Yunus’s argument that small loans to poor women can reduce poverty and empower them, and give one criticism of this argument.
items.answer: Yunus founded the Grameen Bank, lending mainly to poor women in Bangladesh. Criticism: Critics found some borrowers fell into debt and men controlled the loans.
items.markingKey: Up to 2 marks for explaining the view (Neoliberalism); up to 2 marks for an explained criticism. [4]

items.stem: UNESCO figures for girls’ secondary enrolment in three countries are shown below. Table: girls enrolled in secondary school (%) | 2000 | 2020. Country A | 29% | 57%. Country B | 47% | 63%. Country C | 69% | 81%. By how many percentage points did the figure for Country B change between 2000 and 2020?
items.answer: +16 percentage points
items.markingKey: 63 − 47 = +16 percentage points. [1]

items.stem: Kenji is planning a study of girls’ school enrolment across countries. Explain two limitations of using structured interviews for this research.
items.answer: 1. The interview is an artificial social encounter, so answers may not reflect real behaviour. 2. The fixed schedule cannot follow up interesting answers, so data lacks depth.
items.markingKey: For each limitation: 1 mark identified, 1 mark explained and applied to girls’ school enrolment across countries. [4]

items.stem: The table shows official data on girls’ secondary school enrolment in three countries. Table: girls enrolled in secondary school (%) | 2000 | 2020. Country A | 29% | 55%. Country B | 44% | 55%. Country C | 68% | 80%. (a) Calculate the gap between Country A and Country C in 2000 and in 2020, and state whether it narrowed or widened. (b) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that development is empowering women.
items.answer: (a) 2000: 39 percentage points; 2020: 25 percentage points; the gap narrowed. (b) Evidence from the data: The figure rose for Country A, Country B, Country C; Country C had the highest figure for 2020. Changing attitudes to girls’ education and marriage. Qualifications: Enrolment is not the same as completion or quality; education may not lead to jobs; power within households may be unchanged. The data also come from official statistics of 3 girls in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each gap (39 and 25); 1 mark for “narrowed”. [3] (b) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or own knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses the data and own knowledge to argue for and against, with a judgement. [4]

items.stem: Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using structured interviews to research the effects of microfinance on women’s lives.
items.answer: Strengths: answers can be quantified and compared between social groups; every respondent is asked the same questions in the same order, so results are standardised and reliable. Limitations: the interviewer’s presence may produce interviewer bias or socially desirable answers; the fixed schedule cannot follow up interesting answers, so data lacks depth. Theory: structured interviews are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the effects of microfinance on women’s lives but best combined with another method such as non-participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (3-4): some explained strengths or limitations, weakly applied. Level 3 (5-6): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context, using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, ethics). Level 4 (7-8): well-developed, balanced evaluation applied to the context, with theoretical links (positivism/interpretivism) and a reasoned conclusion. [8]

items.answer: Androcentrism

items.stem: Explain what sociologists mean by “postcolonial feminism”, and give one example.
items.answer: A perspective criticising Western feminism for treating women in developing countries as passive victims. Example: Mohanty’s critique of “Third World woman” stereotypes.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition (a perspective criticising Western feminism for treating women in developing countries as passive victims); 1 mark for a relevant example such as Mohanty’s critique of “Third World woman” stereotypes. [2]

items.stem: A Western charity’s advertisement shows women in a village near Nairobi as helpless victims, although the women run a successful savings cooperative. Suggest how a radical feminist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Radical feminism: development is patriarchal: it extends male control over women and nature (Shiva).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: Chloe is planning a study of how charity advertisements represent women. Explain one strength and one limitation of using self-completion questionnaires for this study.
items.answer: Strength: large samples allow patterns and trends across social groups to be measured. Limitation: closed questions impose the researcher’s categories and cannot explore the meanings behind answers, which lowers validity.
items.markingKey: For each: 1 mark identified; 1 mark explained in the context of how charity advertisements represent women. [4]

items.stem: Tariq, a sociology student, is designing a project on how women farmers experience development projects. Explain one strength of using participant observation for this research.
items.answer: It can give access to groups that would never complete a questionnaire, such as deviant subcultures.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying a relevant strength; 1 mark for explaining it in the context of how women farmers experience development projects. [2]

items.stem: A Western charity’s advertisement shows women in a village near Dhaka as helpless victims, although the women run a successful savings cooperative. Explain how a radical feminist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Radical feminism: development is patriarchal: it extends male control over women and nature (Shiva).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: A Western charity’s advertisement shows women in a village near Mexico City as helpless victims, although the women run a successful savings cooperative. Compare how Marxist feminist and liberal feminist sociologists might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Marxist feminism: development under capitalism exploits women’s paid and unpaid labour for profit. Liberal feminism: development must include women equally in training, education and resources; projects have been gender blind (Boserup).
items.markingKey: Up to 3 marks for each perspective: 1 mark for its key idea, 1 mark for applying it to the situation, 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. 1 further mark for a clear point of contrast is included within the 6. [6]

items.stem: Assess how useful content analysis is for studying how charity advertisements represent women.
items.answer: Strengths: it allows representations to be compared over time or between different media; quantitative content analysis using a coding sheet can be repeated by another researcher, so it is reliable. Limitations: coding categories reflect the researcher’s own interpretation, so different coders may disagree; counting images or words may miss their deeper meaning and context. Theory: content analysis is favoured by positivist (quantitative content analysis) or interpretivist (qualitative content analysis) sociologists and produces quantitative or qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying how charity advertisements represent women but best combined with another method such as unstructured interviews (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-3): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (4-6): explained strengths or limitations with some application. Level 3 (7-8): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, practical and ethical issues). Level 4 (9-10): balanced, well-applied evaluation with theoretical links, comparison with an alternative method and a reasoned conclusion. [10]

items.stem: Which term describes an area where TNCs set up factories for export with tax breaks and weak regulation?
items.answer: Export processing zone (EPZ)
items.markingKey: Export processing zone (EPZ): an area where TNCs set up factories for export with tax breaks and weak regulation. [1]

items.stem: State one effect of factory employment on women in developing countries.
items.answer: Greater bargaining power in the household.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a valid point, e.g. greater bargaining power in the household. [1]

items.stem: Explain Elson and Pearson’s argument that TNCs employ young women because they are seen as cheap, docile and “nimble-fingered”, and give one criticism of this argument.
items.answer: Elson and Pearson argued gender stereotypes are used to justify low pay for women in world market factories. Criticism: Some women gain independence and income from factory work.
items.markingKey: Up to 2 marks for explaining the view (Marxist feminism); up to 2 marks for an explained criticism. [4]

items.answer: +6 percentage points

items.stem: The table shows official employment data from a country near Madrid with large export factories. Table: percentage of workers who are women | 1995 | 2020. Garment manufacturing | 60% | 73%. Electronics assembly | 54% | 59%. Factory supervisors and managers | 9% | 13%. (a) Calculate the change, in percentage points, for Garment manufacturing between 1995 and 2020. (b) Describe two patterns shown in the data.
items.answer: (a) 73 − 60 = +13 percentage points. (b) The figure rose for Garment manufacturing, Electronics assembly, Factory supervisors and managers; Garment manufacturing had the highest figure for 2020.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for using 60 and 73; 1 mark for +13 percentage points (sign or “rise/fall” needed). [2] (b) 1 mark for each accurate pattern supported by figures from the table. [2]

items.stem: A sociologist in Toronto wants to research the experiences of women working in export factories. Explain two limitations of using semi-structured interviews for this research.
items.answer: 1. Interviewer bias may still affect answers. 2. Samples are usually fairly small, so representativeness is limited.
items.markingKey: For each limitation: 1 mark identified, 1 mark explained and applied to the experiences of women working in export factories. [4]

items.stem: Explain two ways in which globalisation has affected women’s employment.
items.answer: Feminisation of factory work in EPZs; global care chains; growth of service work; informal sector; migration for work.
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-3): one or two simple points, limited sociological knowledge. Level 2 (4-6): explained points using some concepts, studies or theories. Level 3 (7-8): two well-explained, developed points with accurate concepts, studies or theories, clearly applied to the question. Creditworthy: Feminisation of factory work in EPZs; global care chains; growth of service work; informal sector; migration for work. [8]

items.stem: Assess how useful self-completion questionnaires are for studying the changing share of women in global employment.
items.answer: Strengths: large samples allow patterns and trends across social groups to be measured; closed, pre-coded questions produce quantitative data that is easy to compare and turn into statistics. Limitations: closed questions impose the researcher’s categories and cannot explore the meanings behind answers, which lowers validity; response rates are often low, so the sample may become unrepresentative. Theory: self-completion questionnaires are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the changing share of women in global employment but best combined with another method such as non-participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-3): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (4-6): explained strengths or limitations with some application. Level 3 (7-8): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, practical and ethical issues). Level 4 (9-10): balanced, well-applied evaluation with theoretical links, comparison with an alternative method and a reasoned conclusion. [10]

items.answer: Gender Inequality Index (GII)
items.markingKey: Gender Inequality Index (GII): a UN measure of gender inequality in health, empowerment and the labour market. [1]

items.stem: State one barrier to women’s empowerment in developing countries.
items.answer: Lack of education.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a valid point, e.g. lack of education. [1]

items.stem: Explain two ways in which education may empower women in developing countries.
items.answer: Access to paid employment and income; knowledge of health and family planning reduces fertility and child mortality; greater confidence and political participation; delays early marriage.
items.markingKey: 2 marks for each explained way. [4]

items.stem: A research team is investigating the effects of microfinance on women’s lives. Explain one limitation of using participant observation for this research.
items.answer: The researcher may become too involved and lose objectivity (“going native”).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying a relevant limitation; 1 mark for explaining it in the context of the effects of microfinance on women’s lives. [2]

items.stem: The table shows official data on girls’ secondary school enrolment in three countries. Table: girls enrolled in secondary school (%) | 2000 | 2020. Country A | 25% | 50%. Country B | 40% | 52%. Country C | 67% | 74%. (a) Calculate the percentage change in the figure for Country B between 2000 and 2020. Show your working. (b) Calculate the gap between Country B and Country A in 2000 and in 2020, and state whether it narrowed or widened. (c) Explain one limitation of using official statistics to collect data like these.
items.answer: (a) (52 − 40) ÷ 40 × 100 = 30%. (b) 2000: 15 percentage points; 2020: 2 percentage points; the gap narrowed. (c) Interpretivists argue they are social constructions shaped by the decisions of officials and the public.

items.stem: UNESCO figures for girls’ secondary enrolment in three countries are shown below. Table: girls enrolled in secondary school (%) | 2000 | 2020. Country A | 27% | 46%. Country B | 55% | 65%. Country C | 71% | 84%. (a) Calculate the gap between Country B and Country C in 2000 and in 2020, and state whether it narrowed or widened. items.answer: (a) 2000: 16 percentage points; 2020: 19 percentage points; the gap widened. (b) They show patterns but not the meanings or reasons behind them. The data also come from official statistics of 3 girls in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each gap (16 and 19); 1 mark for “widened”. [3] (b) 1 mark for identifying a relevant limitation (validity, representativeness, reliability); 1 mark for explaining it in context. [2] (c) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses data AND sociological knowledge on one side, or both sides thinly. Level 3 (5-6): balanced evaluation using the data, sociological arguments and comment on the validity of the data, with a reasoned conclusion. [6]

items.stem: Which term describes unpaid work, mainly by women, that is not counted in measures such as GDP?
items.answer: Invisible labour
items.markingKey: Invisible labour: unpaid work, mainly by women, that is not counted in measures such as GDP. [1]

items.stem: Distinguish between “ecofeminism” and “gender blindness”.
items.answer: Ecofeminism: a perspective linking the domination of women with the domination of nature. Gender blindness: failure to recognise how men and women are affected differently by policies.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for each accurate definition, showing the contrast. [2]

items.stem: Distinguish between “ecofeminism” and “invisible labour”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Ecofeminism: a perspective linking the domination of women with the domination of nature (e.g. women leading forest protection movements). Invisible labour: unpaid work, mainly by women, that is not counted in measures such as GDP (e.g. collecting water and caring for children).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: Daniel is planning a study of how charity advertisements represent women. Evaluate the use of self-completion questionnaires for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: large samples allow patterns and trends across social groups to be measured; closed, pre-coded questions produce quantitative data that is easy to compare and turn into statistics. items.stem: Amara, aged 19, moved from her village to work in a garment factory near Lisbon; she works 60 hours a week, sends money home and now helps decide how her family spends it. Explain how a radical feminist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Radical feminism: patriarchy continues in the factory: men control women as supervisors, and women still carry the double burden at home.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Kwame is planning a study of the experiences of women working in export factories. Evaluate the use of non-participant observation for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: the researcher stays detached, so is less likely to “go native” and can record more objectively; it records behaviour as it happens rather than relying on people’s accounts. Limitations: the researcher sees what happens but may not understand the meanings behind it; the presence of an observer may change behaviour (the Hawthorne effect). Theory: non-participant observation is favoured by both positivist and interpretivist (depending on how structured it is) sociologists and produces quantitative or qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the experiences of women working in export factories but best combined with another method such as case studies (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Official data on women’s share of jobs in export industries are shown below. Table: percentage of workers who are women | 1995 | 2020. Garment manufacturing | 72% | 82%. Electronics assembly | 55% | 62%. Factory supervisors and managers | 12% | 14%. (a) Calculate the change, in percentage points, for Electronics assembly between 1995 and 2020. (b) Explain one limitation of using official statistics to collect data like these. (c) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that globalisation has improved women’s position in the labour market.
items.answer: (a) 62 − 55 = +7 percentage points. (b) Interpretivists argue they are social constructions shaped by the decisions of officials and the public. (c) Evidence from the data: The figure rose for Garment manufacturing, Electronics assembly, Factory supervisors and managers; Garment manufacturing had the highest figure for 2020. Managerial jobs are still dominated by men (vertical segregation). Qualifications: More jobs do not mean better pay or conditions; women remain under-represented in management; informal work is not recorded. The data also come from official statistics of 3 workers in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for using 55 and 62; 1 mark for +7 percentage points (sign or “rise/fall” needed). [2] (b) 1 mark for identifying a relevant limitation (validity, representativeness, reliability); 1 mark for explaining it in context. [2] (c) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses data AND sociological knowledge on one side, or both sides thinly. Level 3 (5-6): balanced evaluation using the data, sociological arguments and comment on the validity of the data, with a reasoned conclusion. [6]

items.stem: Which term describes small loans to poor people, often women, to start businesses?
items.answer: Microfinance
items.markingKey: Microfinance: small loans to poor people, often women, to start businesses. [1]

items.stem: What is meant by the term “microfinance”?
items.answer: Small loans to poor people, often women, to start businesses.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition: small loans to poor people, often women, to start businesses. [1]

items.stem: Explain the difference between “Women in Development (WID)” and “Gender and Development (GAD)”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Women in Development (WID): an approach that aimed to include women in existing development projects (e.g. training women in new farming techniques). Gender and Development (GAD): an approach focusing on changing unequal gender relations rather than just including women (e.g. projects challenging men’s control of household income).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: A microfinance scheme near Singapore lends small sums to groups of women; after five years many run small shops, but some have handed the loans to their husbands. Suggest how a liberal feminist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Liberal feminism: education, legal rights and access to credit and jobs gradually empower women and promote development (Boserup, Sen).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: The table shows official data on girls’ secondary school enrolment in three countries. Table: girls enrolled in secondary school (%) | 2000 | 2020. Country A | 22% | 46%. Country B | 53% | 76%. Country C | 61% | 68%. By how many percentage points did the figure for Country C change between 2000 and 2020?
items.answer: +7 percentage points
items.markingKey: 68 − 61 = +7 percentage points. [1]

items.stem: The table shows official data on girls’ secondary school enrolment in three countries. Table: girls enrolled in secondary school (%) | 2000 | 2020. Country A | 26% | 55%. Country B | 52% | 71%. Country C | 67% | 72%. (a) Calculate the percentage change in the figure for Country C between 2000 and 2020. Show your working. (b) Calculate the gap between Country C and Country B in 2000 and in 2020, and state whether it narrowed or widened. (c) Describe two patterns shown in the data.
items.answer: (a) (72 − 67) ÷ 67 × 100 = 7.5%. (b) 2000: 15 percentage points; 2020: 1 percentage point; the gap narrowed. (c) The figure rose for Country A, Country B, Country C; Country C had the highest figure for 2020.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for (72 − 67) ÷ 67 × 100; 1 mark for 7.5% (accept 2-3 s.f.). [2] (b) 1 mark each gap (15 and 1); 1 mark for “narrowed”. [3] (c) 1 mark for each accurate pattern supported by figures from the table. [2]

items.stem: The table shows official data on girls’ secondary school enrolment in three countries. Table: girls enrolled in secondary school (%) | 2000 | 2020. Country A | 34% | 57%. Country B | 41% | 58%. Country C | 63% | 74%. (a) Calculate the gap between Country C and Country B in 2000 and in 2020, and state whether it narrowed or widened. (b) Explain one reason why these data may not give a valid picture of girls’ education. (c) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that development is empowering women.
items.answer: (a) 2000: 22 percentage points; 2020: 16 percentage points; the gap narrowed. (b) They are collected for government purposes, so categories may not fit the sociologist’s needs. (c) Evidence from the data: The figure rose for Country A, Country B, Country C; Country C had the highest figure for 2020. Changing attitudes to girls’ education and marriage. Qualifications: Enrolment is not the same as completion or quality; education may not lead to jobs; power within households may be unchanged. The data also come from official statistics of 3 girls in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each gap (22 and 16); 1 mark for “narrowed”. [3] (b) 1 mark for identifying a relevant limitation (validity, representativeness, reliability); 1 mark for explaining it in context. [2] (c) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses data AND sociological knowledge on one side, or both sides thinly. Level 3 (5-6): balanced evaluation using the data, sociological arguments and comment on the validity of the data, with a reasoned conclusion. [6]

items.stem: Which term describes a perspective linking the domination of women with the domination of nature?
items.answer: Ecofeminism
items.markingKey: Ecofeminism: a perspective linking the domination of women with the domination of nature. [1]

items.stem: Briefly explain Boserup’s view that modernisation projects gave technology and training to men and ignored women’s farming roles.
items.answer: Boserup showed development could worsen women’s status.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the idea; 1 mark for developing it: Boserup showed development could worsen women’s status. [2]

items.stem: Explain Boserup’s argument that modernisation projects gave technology and training to men and ignored women’s farming roles, and give one criticism of this argument.
items.answer: Boserup showed development could worsen women’s status. Criticism: Later feminists argued her solutions did not challenge patriarchy.
items.markingKey: Up to 2 marks for explaining the view (Liberal feminism); up to 2 marks for an explained criticism. [4]

items.stem: A time-use diary study of 600 adults in villages near Santiago produced the results below. Table: average hours per day spent on each activity | Women | Men. Paid work | 5 | 8. Unpaid domestic and care work | 6 | 3. Collecting water and fuel | 1 | 1. What is the difference, in hours, between Women and Men for Unpaid domestic and care work (Men minus Women)?
items.answer: -3 hours

items.stem: Evaluate the usefulness of participant observation for studying how women farmers experience development projects.
items.answer: Strengths: it can give access to groups that would never complete a questionnaire, such as deviant subcultures; it is often the only way to study small or closed groups in depth. Limitations: the researcher may become too involved and lose objectivity (“going native”); studies are small-scale and impossible to repeat exactly, so findings are unreliable and hard to generalise. Theory: participant observation is favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produces qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying how women farmers experience development projects but best combined with another method such as self-completion questionnaires (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]
